c_aei-ai-trust-aviation.abstract: Summaries of aviation occurrence reports written by language models can state facts the source narrative does not support, yet review of every claim is impractical. We study a claim-level audit: a text classifier trained on the narratives re-derives each claimed field value, and a one-sided split-conformal threshold, calibrated on false claims, limits the share of false claims accepted to a chosen level. Claims are routed to automatic acceptance, human review or a contradiction flag, and each decision is written to an audit log. We evaluated the method on 27,443 public NTSB records (1974-2007) for four fields: injury level, weather conditions, light condition and mid-air collision. True claims were taken from the structured fields and false claims were made by swapping values; no language model was run. At a 5% target, false claims accepted ranged from 0.041 to 0.059 across fields and both a random split and a temporal split (training to 1994, testing from 2000). Under the random split, 0.938 to 1.000 of true claims were accepted automatically; under the temporal split this fell to 0.878 to 0.969 for injury, weather and light. The limits are constructed rather than model-written claims, four simple fields, US records up to 2007, and a guarantee that holds only under exchangeability. Testing on real model-written summaries is the next step.
c_aei-ai-trust-aviation.draft_note: Claims are built from NTSB structured fields (true) and value-swapped copies (false); no LLM was run. Deadline of this special issue is probably closed - confirm on the ScienceDirect page.

c_machines-fault-prognostics-2027.abstract: Condition monitoring of hydraulic equipment usually returns a single fault label, even when the data resemble nothing seen during training. This study evaluates a diagnosis that returns a set of possible condition grades with a stated confidence and treats an empty set as an out-of-envelope alarm. We use the public UCI data set of a hydraulic test rig (2205 load cycles, 17 sensors, four components: cooler, valve, pump leakage and accumulator), summarise each cycle by six statistics per sensor, and apply a random forest with split-conformal calibration at the 95% level. With random splits of cycles, five-fold accuracy was 0.985 to 0.998 and set coverage was 0.948 to 0.969, with a mean set size below one. When calibration used stable cycles and testing used the 756 cycles flagged as not yet stable, coverage fell to between 0.20 and 0.60, so the guarantee did not survive this shift. However, the share of empty sets rose from 3-5% to 11-73%, which makes the empty set usable as an alarm. All results come from one test rig and no field data were used; the method is a diagnostic aid, not a safety function.
c_machines-fault-prognostics-2027.draft_note: Measured on the public UCI hydraulic data set (scripts/run_experiment.py, outputs/results.json in the private repo). One rig, no field data; coverage guarantee fails under the stable-to-unstable shift and this is stated.
c_machines-fault-prognostics-2027.title: Certified Diagnosis Sets with an Out-of-Envelope Alarm for Hydraulic Condition Monitoring: Evidence from a Public Test-Rig Data Set

c_npic-hmit-isofic-2027.abstract: Diagnosis aids for nuclear-plant operators usually show one predicted accident type, without saying how early that answer can be trusted or what to show when the accident is not one the model knows. We study this on the public NPPAD simulator data set: 315 runs of 12 pressurised-water-reactor accident types, 97 plant variables sampled every 10 s. For windows ending 20 to 600 s after accident insertion we train a random forest on run-level splits and calibrate split-conformal prediction sets at the 95% level, and we map each set to a display state: single diagnosis, candidate list, or no match. Over ten random splits, windows up to 60 s carried almost no usable signal: accuracy was 0.26 and the mean set held 6.3 of 12 types. At 90 s accuracy was 0.96, coverage 0.96, and a single type was shown for 95% of runs and was correct in 94% of runs. A correct single type was shown by 120 s in 95% of runs; 3.5% were never resolved within 600 s. The no-match state failed as a safeguard: when an accident type was withheld from training and calibration, only 2.9% of its runs produced an empty set, and 69% received a single wrong type. The data are simulated from one reactor model, 12 of the 18 published accident types were available as files, and one type has only nine usable runs. No plant data or operator test is reported.
c_npic-hmit-isofic-2027.draft_note: Measured on public NPPAD simulator data (scripts/run_experiment.py, outputs/results.json in the private repo). Simulated, one reactor model, 12 of 18 types; the no-match state failed in the open-set test and this is stated.
c_npic-hmit-isofic-2027.title: How Soon Can an Operator Display Show a Certified Accident Diagnosis? Prediction Sets over Growing Time Windows on Simulated PWR Data

p_aimed.abstract: Introduction: Esophageal cancer (EC) is associated with substantial mortality and challenges in early detection and treatment planning.� Developing clinical artificial intelligence (AI) systems is constrained by limited access to patient data and the need for integrated, explainable, and secure computational tools. We developed INEsCape, an open-source platform integrating machine learning (ML), synthetic data generation, and clinical decision support (CDS) for EC. Methods: INEsCape uses a Python/FastAPI backend and a React-based web interface, with PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, and Docker-supported deployment. Its documented components include synthetic cohort gen eration, public-dataset ingestion and quality control, ML workflows, SHAP-based explainability, model versioning, data-drift monitoring, risk prediction, prognostic scoring, and guideline-based treatment suggestions. Security features include JSON Web Token authentication, role-based access control, and audit logging. The prognostic module was evaluated using a ridge-penalized Cox proportional-hazards model and an internal-external leave- one-cohort-out design across TCGA-ESCA, GSE53624, and ICGC-ESCC.� Performance was assessed using the concordance index (C-index) and three-year area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). The platform architecture is illustrated in Figure 1. Results: The retrospective evaluation included 391 eligible cases. The pooled C-index was 0.616 (95% confi dence interval, 0.572�0.659), and the three-year AUC was 0.659. The repository documents a working software prototype with API and dashboard components. Automated test coverage is approximately 35%, and some security and validation requirements remain incomplete. Summary: INEsCape integrates data generation, ML, prognostic analysis, and CDS within a modular software platform. Preliminary results support further investigation of its prognostic module but do not establish the clinical effectiveness of the complete platform. Independent reproducibility assessment, broader testing, security improvements, and prospective clinical evaluation are needed before clinical deployment.

p_aimed.title: INEsCape: An Open-Source AI Platform for Esophageal Cancer Risk Prediction and Clinical Decision Support

p_ccus.abstract: Objectives/Scope: This paper presents an intelligent energy and carbon management platform designed for olefin and purified terephthalic acid (PTA) petrochemical units. Its objectives are to integrate high-frequency energy data, monitor energy intensity and carbon emissions, support energy-consumption forecasting, and provide operational recommendations. The platform also explores how digital monitoring and optimization workflows can support industrial decarbonization planning and future CCUS readiness. Methods, Procedures, Process: The platform uses a modular Python and FastAPI architecture, a time-series data layer, and a streaming pipeline based on Apache Kafka, with a Kafka-independent demonstration mode. Its design supports energy data ingestion at one record per second, dashboard visualization, and calculation of Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions using configured emission factors. Forecasting components include Extreme Learning Machines (ELM) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models. Virtual sample generation and what-if scenario analysis address limited-data conditions. A real-time advisory optimization workflow generates recommendations for operator review, with explicit approval required before any proposed action is applied. Results, Observations, Conclusions: The current software prototype brings together energy monitoring, carbon-intensity visualization, forecasting interfaces, scenario analysis, and operator-supervised optimization in a unified workflow. Its demonstration configuration can use a synthetic one-second data stream to exercise the dashboard and analytical pipeline without requiring a live plant connection. The design also includes scheduled Scope 1 and Scope 2 reporting, role-based access controls, and audit-oriented approval workflows. These capabilities provide a technical foundation for examining how plant-level energy and emissions information can be organized to identify potential efficiency opportunities and inform decarbonization planning. However, synthetic demonstration data do not establish predictive accuracy, quantified emissions reductions, or operational performance under industrial conditions. Validation with plant measurements, site-specific emission factors, and process-engineering constraints remains necessary before recommendations can be treated as site-specific evidence. The platform is therefore positioned as a digital decision-support approach rather than a carbon-capture technology or a validated CCUS deployment solution. Novel/Additive Information: The paper contributes an integrated software architecture connecting high-frequency energy monitoring, carbon accounting, forecasting, and operator-approved optimization for energy-intensive petrochemical units. It also outlines a practical digital pathway for linking plant-level efficiency analysis with future CCUS planning, while distinguishing prototype capabilities from outcomes that require industrial validation.

p_gs.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease require the interpretation of heterogeneous clinical information, including medical imaging, biomarkers, and cognitive assessments. NeuroPredict-AI is an AI-enabled multimodal clinical decision support framework designed to integrate these information sources within a unified digital health workflow for neurodegenerative disease risk assessment. The framework combines MRI-based feature extraction using convolutional neural networks with machine learning analysis of disease-related biomarkers and cognitive measures, including MMSE and MoCA. An explainability layer is incorporated to support interpretation of model outputs and provide information on the contribution of different input features. The system is also designed to support healthcare interoperability through integration pathways for EHR and PACS environments using HL7/FHIR standards. Current development and testing activities include synthetic and real-based data records. The system remains a research and development framework and has not undergone clinical validation on real-world patient cohorts. Clinical validation using appropriately governed patient data, along with further performance evaluation, remains a required future stage. NeuroPredict-AI is intended to support clinicians by consolidating multimodal neurological information into an interpretable decision-support workflow while maintaining clinical decision-making under professional supervision. The framework provides a foundation for further research into multimodal, explainable, and interoperable AI-assisted clinical decision support for neurodegenerative disease assessment.

p_healthinfo.abstract: Hospitals generate heterogeneous data, including electronic health records, laboratory results, medical images, and real-time clinical event streams. Turning this data into actionable insight is difficult because of fragmented systems, strict privacy requirements, and the operational burden of deploying machine learning in clinical settings. This paper presents an integrated, open, modular health informatics platform that addresses these challenges end to end. The platform ingests CSV, HL7 v2, FHIR R4, and DICOM data into a Medallion-style data lake (Bronze/Silver/Gold on MinIO with Delta/Iceberg support) and a PostgreSQL analytical warehouse. Incremental ETL with schema validation, scheduled orchestration, and full audit logging ensures data quality. Real-time HL7/FHIR events flow through Apache Kafka and a stream processor that generates clinical alerts, delivered to dashboards via WebSocket and to managers via email/SMS. Interoperability profiles cover both national (Iranian Ministry of Health/SEPAS, insurance systems) and international (US Core, IPS, Epic, HAPI) settings. The MLOps layer provides versioned models for readmission, length-of-stay, mortality/sepsis early warning, clinical-note NLP for ICD extraction, and vital-sign monitoring. It includes calibration metrics, drift monitoring, scheduled retraining, department-specific risk thresholds, and SHAP-based explanations to support clinician trust. Privacy and security are built in through JWT/RBAC, MFA, PHI encryption at rest, pseudonymization/anonymization, consent and retention management, and HIPAA/GDPR-aligned compliance controls. Multi-tenancy lets multiple hospitals share one deployment with isolated data, branding, and quota-based billing. The system is containerized and monitored with Prometheus, Grafana, and Loki. We describe the architecture and design decisions and demonstrate the platform on synthetic patient data. We also discuss current limitations and the roadmap, including genomic data, wearable devices, and clinically validated computer-aided diagnosis for medical imaging.

p_ioch.abstract: Reliable interpretation of quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) data is essential for molecular diagnostics. However, variability in assay measurements, laboratory instruments, and kit lots can complicate result interpretation and quality assessment. This work presents an AI-assisted software framework for diagnostic kit data analysis, with an emphasis on quality control, transparent model evaluation, and laboratory decision support. The framework processes labeled diagnostic records containing cycle-threshold (Ct) values, signal-to-noise ratios, amplification efficiency, quality scores, and additional numerical features. A machine-learning pipeline supports binary classification using a Random Forest classifier, with an alternative support vector machine configuration. The prediction workflow provides positive or negative classifications and associated confidence estimates. The repository also includes a pilot dataset of 60 labeled qPCR records, comprising 19 positive and 41 negative samples from three laboratory device types and two kit lots. Available evaluation tools support the calculation of accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC), confusion matrices, and confidence intervals. Device-grouped cross-validation and kit-lot-specific analysis provide a basis for examining generalization and potential sources of performance variation. The current implementation establishes a foundation for evaluating AI-assisted diagnostic data processing under heterogeneous laboratory conditions. Quantitative performance claims require appropriate out-of-fold evaluation and careful assessment of kit-lot robustness. Further testing on independently characterized laboratory samples is needed to determine the framework's generalizability and potential clinical applicability. This work highlights an approach to developing quality-aware AI decision-support software for molecular diagnostic workflows, while identifying the evaluation steps needed before clinical deployment.

p_isct.abstract: Background and Aims CAR-T therapy outcomes depend on patient HLA profile, tumor antigen expression, CAR construct choice, and the risk of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurotoxicity. Selecting a target and construct for each patient is complex, and few tools combine design, response prediction, and clinician-readable explanation in one auditable system. We developed a software platform for personalized CAR-T design and simulation. The aims were to: Integrate patient HLA and antigen data, target selection, CAR design, and response, CRS, and neurotoxicity simulation in one workflow. Provide per-patient explainability and a clinical narrative that physicians can understand. Enforce security and traceability through role-based access control (RBAC) and an audit trail. Validate the integrated system to Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 5, using pre-specified acceptance criteria and independent cohorts. Methodology Design: Software development and in-silico validation study. No real patients or clinical data were used. System: The chain API → database → object storage → trained response model → explainability → treatment protocol → audit log was implemented with JWT authentication and three roles (viewer, clinician, admin). Per-patient explanations use local occlusion attributions. The platform also provides a model-version registry, Prometheus metrics, and an operator dashboard. Data: Synthetic cohorts were used for training and for independent validation. The model had never seen the validation cohorts. One of them was a shifted-site cohort with different antigen density and CAR mix. Primary endpoints (pre-specified criteria): Model performance on the independent cohort and the shifted site: AUC floor, AUC ≥ 90% of the noise ceiling (“oracle”), expected calibration error (ECE), Brier score versus baseline, balanced accuracy, and worst-subgroup AUC. Integrated-system performance: 100% end-to-end success, p95 latency, audit coverage, RBAC matrix, and serving of the trained model. Robustness under 10% input noise, 20% missing antigens, invalid outputs, and seeded reproducibility. Statistical analysis: Cross-validation, sensitivity/specificity with confidence intervals, and calibration assessment. Reproducibility is automated and runs in CI. Acceptance thresholds were revised after the first run, and this is disclosed. The absolute AUC floor was lowered to ≥ 0.60 and balanced accuracy to ≥ 0.55, because the shifted-site oracle AUC was only 0.656. The ceiling-relative criterion (≥ 90% of oracle) remained the main quality bar. Results All pre-specified criteria passed in the final validation run, in the model (independent and shifted-site cohorts), robustness, and integrated-system domains. Adding the domain features max_expression and efficacy_x_max_expr raised the AUC relative to the oracle ceiling from 0.91 to 0.97 on the same site and from 0.92 to 0.94 on the shifted site. Validation exposed and fixed seven defects, including missing RBAC on PHI and therapy endpoints, privilege escalation via self-registered admin roles, incomplete audit coverage, global rather than per-patient explanations, and unsafe production defaults (default secret and authentication off). After the fixes, end-to-end success was 100%, patient reads and key actions were audited with the actor recorded, and the trained model was actually served in the integrated environment. Conclusion The platform reached TRL 5 as an integrated, secure, and explainable decision-support system for CAR-T design and simulation in a simulated operational environment. Because all cohorts were synthetic and generated by the same formula that defines the labels, the results show software correctness and stability under site shift. They do not show biological or clinical validity. CRS and neurotoxicity outputs come from fixed probability tables and are not yet learned or validated. The platform is not a medical device. The next steps toward TRL 6 are validation on de-identified real-world CAR-T data, learning CRS and neurotoxicity models from real outcomes, PHI encryption and compliance work, and a clinician usability study followed by a shadow-mode pilot.

p_spe.abstract: Abstract Objectives/Scope: This paper proposes a novel adaptive data routing system for industrial telecommunication infrastructures in oil and gas fields. The objective is to address the challenge of reliable, cost-effective, and low-latency data transmission across heterogeneous networks (5G, satellite, and industrial Ethernet) in remote and harsh environments. The scope includes real-time monitoring, multi-criteria decision-making, and dynamic failover mechanisms to ensure uninterrupted operation of critical control and monitoring systems. Methods, Procedures, Process: The proposed system employs a multi-layer architecture consisting of: (1) a network monitoring module that continuously measures key parameters (bandwidth, latency, packet loss, cost, and QoS) across all available links; (2) a data classification module that categorizes each data stream based on criticality level (critical vs. non-critical); (3) a dynamic multi-criteria decision-making module using Fuzzy Analytical Hierarchy Process (Fuzzy AHP) to compute real-time utility scores and select the optimal path for each data stream independently; and (4) an adaptive routing module that performs event-driven failover within <50 ms for critical data, while using timeout-based switching for non-critical data. Results, Observations, Conclusions: Preliminary results indicate that the proposed system reduces communication costs by up to 40% by intelligently routing non-critical data through lower-cost links while ensuring critical data (e.g., PLC commands, safety alarms, pressure/temperature sensor readings) are transmitted via the most reliable and lowest-latency path. The system maintains seamless connectivity with automatic failover under 50 milliseconds for critical data streams, eliminating the need for timeout-based recovery and preventing data loss during network degradation. Field simulations in a representative offshore oil platform scenario demonstrated 99.97% uptime for critical data transmission across 5G, satellite, and Ethernet links. The criticality-aware differentiation mechanism significantly reduces false alarms and unnecessary switching events, improving overall network stability. These findings confirm that the system enhances operational resilience, reduces downtime-related costs, and provides a scalable solution for digital transformation in upstream oil and gas operations. Novel/Additive Information: This paper presents a novel integration of Fuzzy AHP-based multi-criteria decision-making with criticality-aware data classification and dual-mode failover (event-driven for critical data, timeout-based for non-critical data) specifically tailored for heterogeneous industrial telecommunication networks. Unlike existing solutions that treat all data equally or rely solely on QoS metrics, this approach introduces cost and criticality as independent decision factors, providing a more comprehensive and adaptive routing solution not previously reported in petroleum industry literature.

s_cmi.abstract: Saliency maps are widely shown next to medical image predictions, yet they are rarely tested for whether they reflect what a model uses. This study presents ExplainGuard, a framework that measures explanation faithfulness with perturbation tests and compares explanation methods with a random map. We applied it to PneumoniaMNIST chest X-ray images at 64×64 pixels (Zenodo). Gradient and gradient×input maps were less faithful than a random map, with a confidence interval that excludes zero, whereas occlusion was more faithful and more stable. The advantage of occlusion is partly structural because its perturbation is of the same kind as the faithfulness metric. No foundation model was evaluated, although this is the topic of the special issue. Conclusions are limited to a small neural-network classifier on low-resolution images: no pretrained medical encoder, no localisation reference such as bounding boxes and no weight-randomisation check were used. The results suggest that faithfulness testing should precede the clinical display of saliency maps.

s_eg.abstract: Machine-learning facies interpretation from well logs rarely states how uncertain each depth is. We present StratGuard, a framework that returns, for every depth, a calibrated set of admissible facies using split conformal prediction, decodes the facies sequence with a learned stratigraphic transition grammar, and refers uncertain depths to a geologist. We evaluated it on two public data sets with splits by well: SEG 2016 (10 Kansas wells, 9 facies) and FORCE 2020 (81 North Sea wells, lithology). With a 0.90 target, mean coverage was 0.904 and 0.889, but coverage in the worst well was only 0.735 and 0.599, and 19 of 81 FORCE wells fell below 0.85, so the marginal guarantee does not hold well by well. Recalibrating the threshold on 100 labelled depths of the new well raised worst-well coverage from 0.74 to 0.88 (SEG 2016) and from 0.60 to 0.82 (FORCE 2020) and cut the FORCE wells below 0.85 from 19 to 6, at the cost of larger sets on FORCE (2.0 to 2.3). Decoding removed all grammar-violating transitions but changed accuracy only slightly (0.531 to 0.547 on SEG 2016; 0.689 to 0.666 on FORCE). Referral worked on FORCE (61.6% of depths referred, accuracy on retained depths 0.855) but was impractical on SEG 2016, where 89% were referred. Certified sets make facies uncertainty explicit, and a small local labelling effort brings the guarantee much closer to a per-well one. Coverage was assessed per well and overall, not per facies class.
s_eg.draft_note: Numbers measured in research/s_eg_stratguard (private repo, branch research-real-data-validation) on SEG 2016 + FORCE 2020; verify FORCE licence; re-run before submission.
s_eg.title: Certified Facies Sets from Well Logs: Conformal Coverage, Per-Well Reliability and Stratigraphic Decoding on the SEG 2016 and FORCE 2020 Data

s_front_nuc.abstract: Machine-learning classifiers for accident identification in nuclear power plants are trained on a fixed list of accident types, but an operator must also be warned when an accident of an unknown type occurs. This study evaluates open-set identification on the NPPAD data set, which comes from PCTRAN simulation (246 runs, 18 accident types) and not from a real plant. We measure the false rejection of known accidents and the detection of accident types that were held out of training. The false rejection of known accidents was about 0.10. The detection of unknown types depended strongly on the type and was on average between 27% and 49%. Open-set methods of this kind have been published before, and we claim no novelty in method. The analysis uses 246 runs and a fixed analysis window and one open-set approach; OpenMax and prototype-based variants were not evaluated. All results come from simulation and not from plant records, so they should be read as an upper bound on field performance. The results show that a simulator-trained classifier cannot yet be relied upon to flag unknown accidents, and the paper discusses the verification and validation needed before any use in an operating plant, where such a system would only support licensed operators.

s_hydro.abstract: Streamflow behaves differently on rising, receding and stable limbs of the hydrograph, and separate models for each state are often proposed. This study tests whether such state gating improves seven-day-ahead forecasts. For five USGS rivers (2000–2024), a global gradient-boosting model with lagged and seasonal features is compared with persistence and with a hard-gated model that selects a state-specific model from the hydrograph state of the current day, using chronological splits, RMSE and Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency. The global model outperformed persistence. The gated model was worse than the global model at all five stations. We report this as a negative result: gating divides the training data into smaller samples and adds no information beyond the lagged and seasonal features. The models use lagged flow and seasonal features only; precipitation and snow forcing, deep-learning learners, the separation of dam-regulated gauges and rolling-origin evaluation with confidence intervals were not included. The benchmark and code are provided so that others can test gating in other basins.

s_hydro.title: Does Hydrograph-State Gating Improve Seven-Day Streamflow Forecasts? A Negative-Result Benchmark on Five USGS Rivers

s_iai.abstract: Industrial AI for drilling and completion depends on dividing continuous log data into zones before further analysis, and change-point segmentation is a natural candidate. This paper evaluates a log-zonation module that was added next to a formation-integrity damage prevention system and is independent of its claimed functions. We tested PELT change-point segmentation against a smoothed-gradient peak baseline on 62 wells of the public FORCE 2020 data set (gamma ray, density, neutron porosity and sonic logs), using stratigraphic group boundaries as a surrogate ground truth, a tolerance of 15 m and one tuning parameter per method chosen on half of the wells. On the other half, the F1 score for boundaries was 0.33 for PELT, 0.30 for the baseline and 0.09 for random boundaries over five splits by well. The advantage of 0.03 is small and no significance test was done; both methods over-segmented, with 9 and 13 predicted boundaries per well against 5 true ones. An earlier test on the SEG 2016 wells had favoured the baseline (0.62 against 0.55), so the ranking depends on the data. We report this neutral result because it shows that, on public wells, a simple baseline is hard to beat for this task. No real formation-damage data were available, so no claim is made about damage prediction. Evaluation on drilling or damage data, a redefinition of the contribution towards formation integrity and significance tests were not part of this study.

s_icmhi.abstract: Machine-learning models for the design of lipid nanoparticles are trained on libraries of related lipids and then applied to new chemical series, where their error estimates may no longer hold. We test whether split conformal prediction intervals remain valid when the test lipids contain components not seen in training. Using the public AGILE library of 1,199 ionisable lipids built from amine, aldehyde and isocyanide components, with measured HeLa transfection, we trained a random forest on Morgan count fingerprints and compared random splits with splits that assign whole component groups to training, calibration or test, for a nominal coverage of 0.90 and 10 repetitions. Random splitting gave a mean coverage of 0.915. Holding out amine components left coverage at 0.921, but holding out aldehyde or isocyanide components lowered it to 0.840 and 0.865, and to 0.58 and 0.62 in the worst repetitions. Intervals were 9% to 26% wider and the root-mean-square error rose from 2.18 to between 2.7 and 2.9. Coverage therefore depends on which component is new and varies strongly between splits, so a single random-split evaluation can overstate the reliability of uncertainty estimates for new lipid series. We provide a reproducible protocol relevant to medical and health informatics applications of AI-designed delivery systems. The study uses one library, one model family and one transfection endpoint; a second regressor and an independent lipid library were not evaluated.
s_icmhi.draft_note: Replaced on the owner's instruction: the earlier coverage of 0.72 could not be reproduced. Numbers come from research/s_icmhi_ipind (AGILE, bowang-lab/AGILE; private market repo). Topic fit with a medical-informatics venue should be checked.
s_icmhi.title: Applicability Domain of Lipid-Nanoparticle Property Models: Conformal Coverage when Whole Lipid Components Are Held Out

s_icqe.abstract: Quantum algorithms for energy materials, such as battery and fuel molecules, often start from the Hartree–Fock (HF) state, but HF becomes a poor approximation of the ground state when bonds are stretched. We quantify this for H2, LiH, BeH2 and H2O in the STO-3G basis (and LiH in 6-31G) with Hamiltonians computed in PySCF, not measured, and compare the squared overlap of the HF determinant with the full-configuration-interaction (FCI) ground state and the entropy of the natural-orbital occupations as indicators of starting-point quality. H2 at 0.74 Å reproduces the literature energy of −1.1373 Ha. The squared overlap falls from 0.98 near equilibrium to 0.50 for H2 at 4 Å, 0.56 for LiH at 4 Å, 0.38 for BeH2 at 3.5 Å and 0.36 for H2O at 2.2 Å. Within each molecule, overlap and entropy were almost perfectly rank-anticorrelated (Spearman −0.99 to −1.0), so combining them in one index adds little information. CCSD(T) agreed with FCI to better than 1 mHa near equilibrium and failed at long distances, where a restricted HF calculation can also converge to a wrong ionic solution; five such points are flagged and excluded, including the extreme LiH distance reported earlier. The study offers a simple, reproducible check of when an HF start is unsuitable. Active spaces for larger molecules, other reference states and a link to specific energy materials were not studied.
s_icqe.draft_note: Numbers from research/s_icqe_stretchwatch (private market repo). The public GitHub page of the article repository described the overlap-times-entropy index before it was made private; the patent attorney must be informed. The study claims no novelty for the index.
s_icqe.title: StretchWatch: Loss of the Hartree–Fock Reference along Bond-Stretching Curves, with Relevance to Quantum Energy Materials

s_iqicsa.abstract: Splitting a power network into two islands can be written as a combinatorial optimisation problem and has been proposed as an application of the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm (QAOA). We compare QAOA, simulated exactly with state vectors, with greedy local search and a spectral heuristic on two IEEE test systems (9 and 14 buses; MATPOWER data distributed with pandapower), with edge weights equal to the active-power flows of an AC power flow. For weighted MaxCut at depths p = 1, 2 and 3, QAOA reached approximation ratios of 0.742, 0.797 and 0.714 on the 9-bus system and 0.760, 0.820 and 0.753 on the 14-bus system, whereas greedy search found the optimum in both (1.00) and the spectral heuristic reached 1.00 and 0.62. The ratio did not increase monotonically with depth, which points to the classical optimiser as the limit. For an islanding objective that adds the power imbalance of an island and requires at least three buses per island, QAOA's expected cost remained close to that of random splits (normalised score 0.10 to 0.31) while single-flip descent found the exact optimum. We report this as a neutral result at this size: the quantum method does not improve on cheap classical baselines. Larger networks (30 buses and more), tensor-network simulation, noise models, other optimisers and hardware data were not evaluated.
s_iqicsa.draft_note: Measured in research/s_iqicsa_qgrid (private repo, branch research-real-data-validation) on pandapower-bundled IEEE case9/case14 with AC power-flow weights; replaces the owner's unit-weight case14 run. Re-run before submission.
s_iqicsa.title: QAOA for Splitting a Power Network into Two Islands: A Comparison with Greedy and Spectral Partitioning on the IEEE 14-Bus Case

s_iqim.abstract: Reliable use of machine-learning predictions in drug discovery requires an estimate of how far a predicted binding affinity can be trusted. We add distribution-free uncertainty intervals to the affinity predictions of a hybrid quantum–classical drug-discovery platform, treating the platform's predictor as a black box. Split conformal prediction gives intervals with a guaranteed marginal coverage, and a Mondrian variant calibrates separately within strata of the predicted value. We evaluated both on 3,884 EGFR molecules with measured activity from ChEMBL, using ten random seeds and both random and scaffold-based splits, for a nominal coverage of 0.90. Coverage was 0.896 (95% interval ± 0.009) for a random split and 0.894 (± 0.014) when whole chemical scaffolds were held out, so the marginal guarantee held under chemical-series shift. The Mondrian variant did not improve it: worst-stratum coverage was 0.870 against 0.868 for the global variant on a random split. Coverage within groups of true activity was weaker, with the worst group at 0.83 for a random split and 0.78 for the scaffold split for both variants, and the intervals were wide (about 2.8 pIC50 units, 3.3 under scaffold shift). We report this as a negative result for stratification and a caution for activity-conditional claims. The study uses one target and a random-forest stand-in for the platform's predictor; a second target and the platform's own predictor were not evaluated.
s_iqim.draft_note: EGFR numbers reproduced in research/s_iqim_hqca (private market repo). The earlier COX-2 numbers were not reproduced and were removed.
s_iqim.title: Distribution-Free Uncertainty Intervals for Binding-Affinity Predictions: Global versus Mondrian Conformal Calibration on EGFR

s_isie.abstract: Digital twins of industrial assets use remaining useful life (RUL) estimates to plan maintenance, but an optimistic estimate can postpone maintenance past failure. We study a lower bound on RUL as an add-on that is separate from the twin: it takes the twin's point estimate and subtracts a calibrated one-sided error quantile, so that maintenance can be planned on a conservative value. The point estimate maps a label-free vibration health index to RUL with a monotone regression; the quantile comes from leave-one-bearing-out predictions on the training bearings. We evaluated the add-on on the four bearings that failed in the public NASA IMS run-to-failure experiments, holding out one failed bearing at a time. The share of overestimating (unsafe) predictions fell from 0.48 for the point estimate to 0.18 for the lower bound, and in the last 48 hours before failure from 0.66 to zero; a constant-life baseline overestimated in 0.75 of all cases. The price was premature alerts: the share of snapshots with an alert more than 192 hours before failure rose from zero to 0.23, mostly on the longest-lived bearing, whose lower bound was low from the start. With only four failed bearings the results are preliminary and the intervals are wide. The method needs no failure labels from the monitored machine and can run on industrial edge hardware.
s_isie.draft_note: Measured in the product repository (research/rul_lower_bound, PR #1) on NASA IMS data; four failed bearings only. Check the data licence and citation (Lee et al. 2007; feature tables by Hora and Rezapour, MIT).
s_isie.title: A Conservative Lower Bound on Remaining Useful Life as an Add-On to an Asset Life-Cycle Digital Twin: Evidence from NASA IMS Bearing Data

s_jimg.abstract: Pharmacogenomic panels are usually designed with allele frequencies measured in European populations, and their value for other populations is rarely quantified. Using the CPIC guideline data for nine genes and nine population groups, we compute the share of actionable (abnormal-function) alleles that a panel designed from European frequencies would not capture. Such a panel misses about 49% of the abnormal alleles in sub-Saharan African populations and about 47% in East Asian populations, against 19% in Europeans. The analysis uses published frequencies and no individual-level data. The analysis does not cover the gene CYP2D6 with its structural variants, was not verified against individual-level data, reports no sampling-based confidence intervals and includes no group close to the Iranian population. The result shows that panel design needs population-specific frequency data to avoid unequal clinical benefit. The topic is genomic rather than imaging, and its fit with this special issue must be confirmed with the editors before submission.

s_jpse.abstract: Operators of storage terminals need forecasts of inventory with a stated uncertainty, but terminal-level tank data are rarely public. As a proxy we use the weekly US crude-oil inventories of the EIA (1982–2026, 2,300 weeks) and test a ridge-regression forecast of the h-week change with split-conformal prediction intervals at horizons of one to four weeks, with a chronological 60/20/20 split. The ridge model reduced the root-mean-square error relative to persistence by 1.2% at one week and by 3.9% at four weeks, a small gain, and the nominal 90% intervals covered 0.81 of the test weeks at one week and 0.88 at four weeks, so they were too narrow at all horizons and closest to nominal at the longest. The data are national inventories and not tank levels, and the journal is about pipelines, so the fit of the study with the journal is weak. The study uses national weekly inventories and no exogenous drivers or consensus forecasts, so its claims are limited to the proxy setting. It shows that a simple interval forecast gives a modest accuracy gain over persistence, that static conformal calibration under-covers on this series, and it sets a reproducible baseline for terminal-level data.
s_jpse.draft_note: Numbers reproduced on 2026-11-01 from the EIA series uploaded by the data task (2,300 weeks, 1982-08-20 to 2026-10-23). s_jpse.title: Conformal Forecast Intervals for Crude-Oil Inventories: Weekly US Data as a Proxy for Terminal-Level Monitoring

s_mie.abstract: Hospital readmission risk models are used to allocate follow-up resources, and calibration of their probabilities is often recommended. We test whether post-hoc recalibration, overall and within subgroups, improves 30-day readmission models for patients with diabetes. Using the public Diabetes 130-US hospitals data (69,990 patients after keeping the first encounter of each patient and excluding deaths and hospice discharges) with patient-level splits, we trained logistic regression and gradient boosting and compared Platt scaling, isotonic regression and temperature scaling, applied globally and within three age groups, over 10 random splits. The models were already well calibrated before any correction: the expected calibration error was 0.005 for logistic regression and 0.006 for gradient boosting, and no recalibration method lowered it; recalibrating within age groups did not help either (error about 0.009 to 0.010 in every variant). Discrimination was modest, with an AUROC of 0.646 and 0.650. We report this as a negative result: for this data set calibration is not the limiting problem and discrimination is. Temporal validation, subgroups other than age and a comparison with published fairness audits were not carried out. The study indicates that calibration auditing should check first whether a model is already calibrated and gives a reproducible benchmark for health informatics.
s_mie.draft_note: Reproduced independently in research/s_mie_readmitcal (private market repo) on the full Diabetes 130 file; 10 seeds with 95% intervals in results.json.
s_mie.title: ReadmitCal: Are 30-Day Readmission Models for Patients with Diabetes Already Calibrated? A Negative Result on 69,990 Patients

s_npj.abstract: Reported accuracy of wearable activity recognition depends on how the data are split. Using the UCI HAR data of 30 subjects, we compare random window splits with subject-level splits. Random splitting overstated accuracy by 3 to 5 percentage points, and some subjects reached only 72% to 79% accuracy. Conformal prediction intervals kept coverage above 0.9 in both settings, so no leakage effect on coverage was seen. The study is small and its fit with this journal is doubtful. The study uses one data set and classical models; confidence intervals over several seeds were not computed, and deep models and free-living or clinical data were not evaluated. We recommend subject-level evaluation and per-subject reporting for digital-health claims based on wearable sensors.

s_oe_call2027.abstract: Maintenance teams offshore usually receive a single fault label from condition-monitoring software, with no statement of confidence and no warning when the machine operates outside the conditions the model has seen. This paper presents HydroGuard, a diagnosis tool that returns the set of possible condition grades for the cooler, valve, pump and accumulator of a hydraulic system at a stated 95% confidence and raises an out-of-envelope alarm when no grade fits. The tool was tested on a public hydraulic test-rig data set (2205 load cycles, 17 sensors) and not on platform data. On random splits of the cycles, five-fold accuracy was 0.985 to 0.998 and coverage was 0.948 to 0.969, with a mean set size below one grade. Where the rig's conditions had not yet stabilised, coverage dropped to between 0.20 and 0.60, so the confidence statement cannot be trusted there; the share of empty sets, however, rose from about 3-5% to 11-73%, so the alarm marks exactly the cycles on which the tool should not be trusted. We propose a work-order rule based on the output: a single confident grade goes to planning, a multi-grade set goes to inspection, and an empty set triggers a check of the operating state before any decision. The rule has not been tested with an operator. The limits are one rig, no offshore field data, and the need to re-calibrate on every new asset. A pilot with an operator on its own historian data is the next step.
s_oe_call2027.draft_note: Measured on the public UCI hydraulic data set (scripts/run_experiment.py, outputs/results.json in the private repo). One rig, no field data; coverage guarantee fails under the stable-to-unstable shift and this is stated. SPE OE27 abstract length: the 2025 rule was 225-450 words; verify the OE27 rule.
s_oe_call2027.title: HydroGuard: Confidence-Stated Fault Diagnosis for Offshore Hydraulic Equipment with an Out-of-Envelope Alarm

s_pet.abstract: Fault detection in oil wells must keep false alarms low while still detecting faults. We study a conformal alarm threshold as an add-on to an artificial-lift management system, using the public Petrobras 3W data, version 2: 1,119 real instances from 40 wells (594 normal, 525 faults of nine types). A robust z-score statistic is computed from seven sensors against a reference taken at the start of each instance, and the threshold is the conformal quantile of the maxima of normal calibration instances at a target false-alarm rate of 0.10. Wells were split between calibration and test in 20 random repetitions. The false-alarm rate on unseen wells was 0.147 on average, but ranged from 0.009 to 0.551 between splits and exceeded the target in half of them; fixed thresholds of z = 5, 10 and 20 gave 0.195, 0.103 and 0.067. Hence the instance-level guarantee does not transfer to new wells, because instances of one well are not exchangeable with those of others. From the labelled onset, alarms were raised for 87% and 96% of the instances of two fault types but for only 9% of the 343 instances of the largest class, which these sensors barely reveal. Alarms before the onset cannot be distinguished from false alarms and are not counted as early warning. Calibration by well and fault-specific sensors are needed. The threshold was compared with fixed thresholds only; other detectors such as Isolation Forest or CUSUM were not evaluated.
s_pet.draft_note: Measured in research/s_pet_intellilift (private repo, branch research-real-data-validation) on 3W v2 real instances; replaces the owner's earlier 114-instance run. Check the 3W version/licence citation and re-run before submission.
s_pet.title: Conformal Alarm Thresholds for Oil-Well Fault Detection on Real Petrobras 3W Data: A Well-Level Evaluation of False-Alarm Control and Detection

s_ps.abstract: Soft sensors that estimate the melt index of polyethylene online are proposed to replace delayed laboratory results, but to be useful they must beat the simplest baseline. On the public sequential-reactor multi-grade (SRMG) industrial data (331 samples, four grades; research use only, after Liu, Gao and Chen, 2013) we compared ridge regression, random forest and just-in-time (nearest-neighbour) learning with a baseline that repeats the last laboratory value of the same grade, using one-step-ahead rolling-origin evaluation over the last 166 samples. For the final melt index (normalised units) the baseline had a root-mean-square error of 0.0426 (R² 0.32); just-in-time learning reached 0.0412 (R² 0.37), random forest 0.0441 and ridge regression 0.171. At the 14 grade-transition samples the baseline error rose to 0.106 and ridge regression had the lowest error (0.079), while random forest (0.106) was no better than the baseline and just-in-time learning was in between (0.088). The sample is small, the data are normalised and the results are from one process, so the conclusion is limited: apart from a marginal gain by just-in-time learning, no soft sensor clearly beat the baseline over all samples, and grade transitions are the only place where a model improved on it.
s_ps.draft_note: Results produced on 2026-11-01 from the SRMG file uploaded by the data task. They replace the earlier design-only text. No manuscript exists yet for this venue. Data licence: academic research only.
s_ps.title: Soft Sensing of Melt Index in Multi-Grade Polyethylene Production: Benchmarking against the Last-Laboratory-Value Baseline

s_qip.abstract: Estimating the expectation value of a Hamiltonian on a quantum computer requires many repeated measurements, and the way a fixed budget of shots is divided among the Pauli terms determines the accuracy of the estimate. We compare uniform allocation, allocation weighted by coefficient magnitude and random-Pauli classical shadows at equal total shot budget for the ground states of H2 (4 qubits, 14 Pauli terms) and LiH (12 qubits, 630 terms) in the STO-3G basis. The Hamiltonians are computed with PySCF and OpenFermion and not measured on a device, because no public hardware measurement data set was found. Variances of the term-wise allocations were computed exactly and those of the shadows by Monte Carlo. Relative to uniform allocation, weighting by coefficient magnitude lowered the root-mean-square error by 14% for LiH but raised it by 35% for H2, and classical shadows gave about three times the error of uniform allocation for both molecules. An oracle allocation that uses the unknown state reached 0.57 (LiH) and 0.75 (H2) of the uniform error, and no scheme without grouping reached chemical accuracy (1.6 mHa) for LiH at 10^6 shots (best: 5.9 mHa without the oracle). The poster will show the protocol, this negative result for shadows and the limits of a simulation-only study. Grouping of commuting terms, larger molecules and hardware noise were not evaluated; we make no claim about performance on hardware.
s_qip.draft_note: Measured in research/s_qip_shotlab (private repo, branch research-real-data-validation) with PySCF/OpenFermion Hamiltonians; replaces the earlier claim of 11-12% lower RMSE for weighted allocation and shadows, which the exact variances do not support. Re-run before submission.
s_qip.title: Shot-Budget Allocation for Pauli-Sum Observables: A Simulation Study of Weighted Allocation and Classical Shadows
